Other bacteria isolated include Haemophilus influenzae and atypical Mycobacte- ria spp. Various diagnostic methods are available1-3 and clinical di- agnosis of cystic fibrosis may be confirmed by establish- ing that chloride concentrations in sweat are raised. This may be done by using the pilocarpine sweat test (see Pilo- carpine, p.1885). Identification of gene mutation is possi- ble and may be used for further confirmation of the diag- nosis and identification of carrier status.4 In some areas neonatal screening programs have been instituted, to allow for early intervention. Antibacterials 167 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) The reduced morbidity and improved survival in patients with cystic fibrosis are largely due to the management of pulmonary disease with antibacterials and physiotherapy and to nutritional management. Several reviews have dis- cussed both established and experimental therapy.5-9 De- spite the successes, the evidence base for some procedures is scanty,9 and there may be variations in management be- tween centres. However, the cornerstones of current man- agement are:8,9 • mechanical airway clearance, with the use of adjuncts such as dornase alfa and hypertonic saline • prevention or eradication of pulmonary infections in early disease • suppression of bacterial load through antibacterial treat- ment of chronic infection in more advanced disease • use of ibuprofen or azithromycin to control lung inflam- mation • aggressive antibacterial treatment of pulmonary exacer- bations • nutritional support to ensure an adequate intake of calo- ries and salt, with supplementation of pancreatic en- zymes and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K • maintaining regular physical activity Airway clearance by manual chest percussion and me- chanical techniques including chest-wall or airway oscilla- tion helps to loosen secretions and aid their removal. Dor- nase alfa10 is given by aerosol inhalation and reduces the viscosity of the sputum by breaking down the large quan- tities of DNA released by degenerating inflammatory cells. The use of dornase alfa has been associated with some improvement in lung function and it might be a use- ful adjunct to bronchial drainage, although it is unclear whether it prevents the development of progressive lung damage.
